blocks.text: Design a cloud file storage and sync platform like Google Drive, keeping a user's files available and synchronized across every device they use, while storing an enormous, ever-growing volume of files as efficiently as possible. Two problems make this genuinely distinct from this project's other storage designs: most file versions share the overwhelming majority of their content with the version before them, wasting storage if each version is stored in full, and two devices can genuinely edit the exact same file offline at the same time, in a way no automatic merge can safely resolve for an arbitrary file, unlike this category's earlier real-time, structured document co-editing design.

blocks.alt: A file is split into content-addressed chunks so only genuinely new content is stored, and when two devices edit the same file offline, whichever syncs first becomes canonical while the other is preserved as a separate conflict copy rather than lost

blocks.text: The two techniques that solve these are content-addressable, chunk-based storage with deduplication, splitting a file into chunks identified by their own content hash so identical chunks across versions and even across different files are only ever stored once, and conflict copies, when a sync detects a genuinely divergent, offline edit, it preserves the losing edit as a separate file rather than attempting a risky, arbitrary-file automatic merge or silently discarding it.

blocks.text: A user should be able to upload a file and have it stored efficiently, without paying the full storage cost again for content that already exists elsewhere in the system. A user should be able to sync files across multiple personal devices, with edits on one device eventually reaching every other device. When two devices edit the same file offline before either has seen the other's change, both edits should be preserved, never silently lost. A user should be able to share a specific file or folder with specific other people at a specific permission level.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and the first two are the genuinely hard, real problems this design centers on.

blocks.alt: Storage efficiency across versions and users, never silently losing an edit, reliable multi-device sync, fast uploads even for very large files, and controlled, granular sharing

blocks.text: Storage efficiency means two files, or two versions of the same file, sharing most of their content should not cost anywhere close to double the storage. Never silently losing an edit means two people editing the same file offline must never result in one of those edits simply vanishing without a trace. Reliable multi-device sync means a change made on one device should reliably reach every other device that file is synced to. Fast uploads even for large files means a small edit to a huge file should never require re-uploading the entire thing from scratch. And controlled, granular sharing means access to any given file or folder must be precisely controllable, per person or per group, not all-or-nothing.

blocks.text: This design assumes files are edited by one person at a time per session, offline-capable but not simultaneously co-edited character by character, real-time collaborative editing is treated as this category's separate, already-covered structured document design's own concern. A genuine offline edit conflict is assumed to always produce a separate conflict copy rather than an automatic merge, since this design covers arbitrary file types, not just text where a real merge might be meaningful. Chunking is assumed content-defined rather than strictly fixed-size, so a small edit shifts only the chunks actually near the edit, not every subsequent chunk in the file.

blocks.text: A platform at real scale might store billions of files across an enormous number of users. Deduplication commonly saves a substantial share of total raw storage, since so many file versions, and even files from different users, share large amounts of identical content, common document templates, duplicate copies, and repeated edits to the same underlying file. A typical user syncs files across several personal devices, and while genuine offline edit conflicts are comparatively rare relative to total sync volume, they must never be silently lost when they do occur.

blocks.text: An uploaded file passes through a chunker that splits it into content-addressed pieces, storing only the chunks not already present anywhere in the chunk store and committing the resulting chunk list as a new file version. The sync service tracks each file's current canonical version, and when a device's sync request reveals its edit was based on a version that has since changed, a conflict handler preserves that edit as a separate conflict copy rather than overwriting or attempting to merge it.

blocks.alt: A file is chunked and deduplicated against the existing content-addressable store, and a sync service tracks each file's canonical version, routing a genuinely divergent offline edit to a conflict handler that preserves it as a separate copy

blocks.text: Every chunk is identified by a hash of its own content, and a chunk is only ever actually stored the first time that exact content is seen anywhere in the system, any later file, or any later version of the same file, that happens to contain the identical chunk simply reuses the existing stored copy.

blocks.alt: A chunk identified by its own content hash is stored only the first time it is seen; any later occurrence of that exact content, anywhere, simply reuses the already-stored chunk

blocks.text: When a large, already-synced file receives a small edit, only the chunks actually near that edit end up with a genuinely new content hash, every other, unchanged chunk keeps its original hash and needs no new upload or storage at all, dramatically reducing the cost of syncing a small change to a large file.

blocks.alt: A small edit changes the content hash of only the chunks actually near it, so only those specific chunks need to be uploaded, while every unchanged chunk is simply reused

blocks.text: When two devices edit the same file offline starting from the same version, whichever syncs first becomes the new canonical version. When the second device syncs its own edit, the service detects that its starting version no longer matches the current canonical one and, rather than silently overwriting or attempting a risky automatic merge, preserves that edit as a separate, clearly labeled conflict copy file.

blocks.alt: File tracking its current canonical version, FileVersion recording which prior version it was based on, Chunk holding deduplicated content by hash, and ChunkReference linking a version to its ordered chunks

blocks.text: ChunkReference is the join that lets many different file versions, even across entirely different files, all point to the exact same underlying Chunk row without that content ever needing to be duplicated in storage.
blocks.content: ChunkReference is the join that lets many different file versions, even across entirely different files, all point to the exact same underlying Chunk row without that content ever needing to be duplicated in storage.

blocks.text: Chunks are modeled as a separate, globally shared table keyed purely by content hash, deliberately decoupled from any specific file, since the entire deduplication benefit depends on the exact same chunk being reusable across unrelated files, not just across versions of one file. FileVersion's own basedOnVersionId column is what makes conflict detection a simple, direct comparison, rather than needing to infer divergence from timestamps or a more complex vector clock scheme.

Two devices editing the same file offline: the first sync becomes canonical, and the second, divergent one is preserved as a separate conflict copy

blocks.text: The happy path is the upload flow above, a file cleanly chunked, deduplicated, and committed. The workflow worth walking through separately is the conflict flow, both devices genuinely believed they were editing the current version when they went offline, and neither one is simply wrong, the sync service does not try to guess which edit is more correct, it accepts the first sync as canonical and honestly preserves the second as its own separate file, leaving the actual decision about which content to keep entirely up to the person who made both edits.

blocks.alt: A device's own already-cached local chunks are used directly; chunks not yet cached locally are fetched from the chunk store and cached for next time

blocks.text: Because most of a synced file's chunks do not change between edits, a device that already has most of a file cached locally only ever needs to fetch the small number of chunks that genuinely changed, rather than re-downloading the entire file on every sync.

blocks.alt: A file change on one device is queued for propagation, and sync workers notify every other device that file is synced to

blocks.text: Queuing sync propagation lets it happen asynchronously across however many devices a file is shared with, without the original uploading device needing to wait on every single other device actually receiving the update.

blocks.alt: A file operation is routed by hashing the file id, so every operation on one file is always handled consistently

blocks.text: Partitioning by file id keeps a specific file's version history and conflict detection logic strictly local to one partition, letting an especially large or frequently-edited file be handled without needing coordination across every other file on the platform.

blocks.alt: Chunk store growth outpacing expectations, or rising sync propagation latency, triggers adding more chunk storage or sync worker capacity

blocks.text: Because deduplication keeps total chunk storage growing far more slowly than raw upload volume, scaling the chunk store itself is comparatively gentle, while sync propagation capacity scales more directly with active device and edit volume.

blocks.text: The chunk store is partitioned by content hash and grows slowly thanks to deduplication, a very different growth curve from this project's object storage design, where every object's data is genuinely unique. File version metadata is partitioned by file id and grows with edit volume rather than raw data volume, since a version's row only records chunk references, not chunk content itself.

blocks.alt: A file's current canonical version is strongly consistent, exactly one canonical version at a time per file; a specific device's own local sync state is eventually consistent, catching up asynchronously as it reconnects

blocks.text: This split is what lets a device work offline at all, its own local state is allowed to lag the true canonical version until it next syncs, while the canonical version itself, the thing conflict detection is actually checked against, always stays a single, unambiguous source of truth.

blocks.alt: A large file's chunk upload interrupted partway through resumes from the last successfully stored chunk rather than restarting from the very beginning

blocks.text: Because a file is uploaded as a set of independent, individually-addressable chunks rather than one monolithic byte stream, an interruption only ever costs the chunks not yet confirmed stored, not the entire upload, making even a very large file's upload naturally resumable.

blocks.alt: A request to view or edit a file or folder is checked against that specific person or group's granted permission level; an unauthorized request is denied outright

blocks.text: Granular, per-file and per-folder sharing is this design's defining security concern, distinct from this project's bucket-level object storage design, since a personal file storage platform genuinely needs fine-grained control, a user sharing one specific document with one specific collaborator, not an all-or-nothing bucket permission model.

blocks.text: Deduplication ratio, how much of total logical storage is actually saved by chunk reuse, is a clear, ongoing signal of whether the storage-efficiency mechanism is working as designed. Conflict copy creation rate is worth watching too, a sudden spike for a specific user or file often points to a genuine, ongoing offline-editing pattern worth understanding rather than an isolated, one-off event.

blocks.text: Content-addressable chunking paired with conflict copies, rather than attempted automatic merging, is the right default because it is honest about what this design can and cannot safely do, deduplication is a genuine, mechanical win regardless of file type, while merging an arbitrary binary file is not something that can be done safely at all.

blocks.text: Content-addressable deduplication is the largest cost optimization in this entire design, directly reducing total storage in proportion to how much content genuinely repeats across versions and users. Incremental, chunk-level uploads avoid the far larger bandwidth and storage cost of re-uploading an entire large file for even the smallest edit.

blocks.text: A change to the chunking algorithm itself needs careful, gradual rollout, since a poorly chosen chunk boundary strategy can quietly erode deduplication effectiveness across the entire platform without causing any single, obvious failure. Conflict detection logic changes deserve equal caution, a bug that fails to detect a genuine divergence risks silently overwriting one user's edit with another's, exactly the failure this design exists to prevent.

items: Architecture: content-addressable chunk deduplication feeding a sync service that tracks each file's canonical version, with a conflict handler preserving divergent offline edits as separate copies.
Capacity: billions of files across an enormous user base, substantial storage savings from deduplication, and rare but never-to-be-lost offline edit conflicts.
The core techniques: content-addressable chunk deduplication and conflict-copy detection, both worked through with a real, verified implementation in Java, Python, and C++.
Database: a globally shared, content-hash-keyed chunk store decoupled from any specific file, alongside file-partitioned version metadata tracking lineage.
End-to-end workflows: a normal upload-and-deduplicate flow and a genuine offline conflict flow, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: a strongly consistent, single canonical version per file, paired with an eventually consistent, per-device local sync state.

Trade-offs: content-addressable chunking with conflict copies versus storing every full version separately versus attempting automatic merging for every file type, compared directly on storage cost and safe conflict handling.
